title: The Skybridge Rescue
audienceRationale: Age 9 / grade 3 sits exactly at the equal-groups-to-fluent-multiplication transition, so physicalized factors (a group-size dial and a group-count dial) match their developmental need to keep multiplication grounded in countable structure while the disguised framings push toward abstraction. Text is minimal and story is carried by animation and sound, keeping reading load near zero. The rescue premise offers prosocial stakes appropriate to the age, and challenge deepens through representational novelty rather than bigger numbers, matching grade-3 fact ranges.
openingPromise: A floating mountain city has snapped its skybridges in a storm, stranding families on drifting islands. You are the newly hired Bridgewright, and your crane can only lift plank bundles in equal groups. If you calculate the load right, whole bridge spans slam into place and stranded islanders run across to safety before their island drifts out of reach.
firstThreeSeconds: The screen opens mid-crisis: wind howls, an island with three waving villagers tilts and drifts, and a glowing crane hook swings toward the player with a bundle counter reading "0 planks loaded." A single pulsing gap in the bridge shows exactly how many planks are needed via faint ghost-plank outlines, inviting the child to grab the hook immediately.
firstAction: The child drags the crane hook onto a plank pallet and taps the bundle dial to choose "bundles of 4," then taps "load 3 bundles." The crane visibly clips 3 bundles of 4 planks, swings across the chasm, and the planks snap into the 12-slot gap one group at a time — a perfect fit, the span glows, and the first villager sprints across cheering.
interactionDemonstration: Correct completion of a span requires producing an exact product from a chosen group size and group count under a novel framing, so each successful crane run is direct behavioral evidence of transferring equal-groups reasoning: the child cannot succeed by pattern-matching a familiar array picture, because the requirement is expressed as seats, weights, knots, or split cargo, and the controls force explicit selection of both factors.
coreInteraction: Every rescue is a live loading puzzle: each broken span shows a gap with a total slot count presented in an unfamiliar framing (ghost outlines, a weight limit, a rope-knot pattern, cargo crates per gondola), never as a bare multiplication prompt. The child sets two physical controls — bundle size and number of bundles — and fires the crane. The planks install group by group in real time, so the child watches equal groups accumulate toward the total. Exact fit completes the span; underload leaves a visible hole villagers refuse to cross; overload makes extra planks tumble into the clouds and the span sag under excess weight. The child reads each new situation, decides what the "group" is and how many are needed, and expresses it through machinery rather than answer buttons.
mathAsPower: Equal-groups multiplication IS the crane's operating system. The world only changes when the product is right: 4 bundles of 5 lantern-poles lights a night crossing, 6 gondolas carrying 3 children each empties an island exactly, a weight limit of 24 forces the child to invent 4×6 or 6×4 or 8×3 and see each choice build a differently-shaped but equally strong span. Wrong products produce physically legible consequences — gaps, sag, tumbling planks — so the math is felt as structural force, not scored as an answer. Decomposition becomes a tool: a 15-slot gap with only bundles-of-5 pallets available teaches the child to reason "3 groups of 5" under a new disguise every time.
stakes: Each island has a visible drift meter; every crane cycle nudges the island farther from the city. Villagers react in real time — cheering as spans grow, clutching hats and pointing anxiously at gaps. The stakes are rescue-based and warm, never punitive: the pressure is "get them home," and the drift meter creates urgency without a hard fail-lockout on early spans.
consequences: Underloading leaves a visible hole; a villager walks up, peers into the gap, shakes their head, and the ghost outlines of the missing planks flash — showing exactly how many more are needed as a countable remainder, not a red X. Overloading makes surplus planks tumble dramatically into the clouds and the span groan and sag; the crane operator character winces and taps the load dial, cueing the child to compare their product to the requirement. If an island drifts past the far marker, the crane extends an emergency zip-line: the rescue still succeeds but slowly and without the triumphant span-completion fanfare, preserving dignity while making precision feel worth it.
recovery: After any miss, the world itself teaches: the gap re-renders with the already-placed groups highlighted and the remainder outlined, and the companion crane-bird lands on the dial and physically pecks it once per group while the child counts along — a group-wise recount, never a spoken answer. The child adjusts either dial and refires immediately; there is no restart, only re-loading. Two consecutive misses on a span slow the drift meter and add a subtle group-boundary shimmer to the requirement so the structure becomes easier to parse, then fade that scaffold on the next span.
progression: Span 1 — Ghost Planks: the gap shows 12 faint plank outlines arranged in 3 rows; only bundles of 4 are available, so the child must see 3 groups of 4 hiding in the structure and load 3×4.

Span 2 — The Gondola Evacuation: no planks this time; 18 stranded villagers, each gondola seats 6. The same equal-groups reasoning transfers to trips: how many gondola runs empty the island exactly, with leftover villagers visibly stranded if the child under-plans.

Span 3 — The Weight-Limit Bridge: the gap displays only a total load rating of 20 stone-weight and pallets in bundles of 5. The child must produce the total from groups without any visual array, loading 4 bundles of 5 and watching the load meter fill in equal jumps.

Span 4 — The Knot Rope Ladder: a rescue rope needs knots tied in a repeating pattern, 7 sections with 3 knots per section; the child sets the knotting machine and predicts the total (21) before firing, then watches the count confirm groupwise.

Span 5 — The Split Cargo Finale: two islands drift at once; 24 supply crates must be divided into two crane runs using different bundle sizes (e.g., 4 bundles of 3 to one island, 2 bundles of 6 to the other), proving flexible transfer: same total, different equal-group structures, both spans completing simultaneously in a double rescue.
interactionContinuity: The bundle-dial-and-fire loop is identical across all five spans; only the situation wrapping the equal-groups structure changes. This keeps mechanical load flat so all new cognitive work is the transfer itself, and the finale composes the same loop twice concurrently rather than introducing a new mechanic.
worldReaction: The world is the scoreboard: spans physically exist or don't, villagers cross or wait, islands reconnect one by one into a visible restored city, and the drift meter, load meters, and lantern ceremony all read directly off the child's products. Every correct equal-groups computation adds permanent structure to the world; every miss changes the world legibly (holes, sag, drift) without erasing progress.
payoff: The final double rescue joins all islands back to the city: every rescued villager gathers on the completed skybridge network for a lantern-lighting ceremony where lanterns rise in equal groups matching the child's actual builds (their 3×4 span releases 3 clusters of 4 lanterns). The city stamps the child's Bridgewright license with an emblem built from the group structures they used, making their specific mathematical choices the literal shape of the reward.
replayVariation: On replay, span requirements are procedurally regenerated with new totals, new bundle sizes, and rotated framings (seats, weights, knots, crates, lantern hooks), and the finale swaps which constraint is fixed — sometimes bundle size is locked and the child chooses count, sometimes the reverse, sometimes total load must be split across two runs differently. Island layouts, weather, and villager casts reshuffle so the story feels fresh while the transfer construct — recognize the equal-group structure inside an unfamiliar situation — is retested with entirely new items each run, never reusing prior item content.
visualDirection: Warm storybook-painterly skyworld: teal-and-gold dusk sky, chunky wooden islands with mossy edges, glowing amber lanterns, and a friendly brass crane with big readable dials. Equal groups are always visually literal — bundles are wrapped with a visible count band, planks install in distinct group-colored clusters that settle into a unified span, and the gap's requirement is embedded in the scenery (outlines, meters, seats) rather than floating UI text. High contrast, large tap targets, characters with expressive silhouette animation so a 9-year-old reads the story without any text.
motionDirection: Slow, weighty crane swings with satisfying easing; planks snap into slots with a small squash-and-stretch bounce, one group landing per beat so grouping is temporally readable. Islands bob gently on a sine drift; villagers have quick, joyful run cycles across finished spans. Failure motion is comic and soft — tumbling planks pinwheel into fluffy clouds with a poof. Camera pulls back on each completed span to show the growing network, reinforcing accumulation.
soundDirection: Wind bed with soft creaking wood; a rising three-note motif plays per group as planks land, and a resolved chord completes an exact-fit span — the harmony literally resolves only when the product is correct. Underload gets a hollow wooden knock on the empty slot; overload gets a descending slide-whistle as planks tumble. Villager cheers scale with rescue size. Dial clicks are tactile and per-unit so setting "4 bundles" produces four distinct clicks.
usefulLibraries: PixiJS for performant 2D layered sky-world rendering and sprite group animation
GSAP for crane swing easing, squash-and-stretch plank landings, and camera pull-backs
Howler.js for layered wind bed, per-group musical motif, and resolving completion chords
matter-js (lightweight use) for tumbling overload planks and island bobbing physics feel
engagementPrediction: A 9-year-old third grader is predicted to engage strongly with the rescue urgency, tactile crane machinery, and visible group-by-group construction; the soft-failure design (zip-line, remainder outlines) should sustain persistence through the harder disguised framings in spans 3–5, with the split-cargo finale producing the peak challenge and pride moment. Predicted session length 8–12 minutes with high refire rate after misses rather than abandonment.
falsifyingEvidence: The design fails its purpose if: (a) children succeed on spans 3–5 only after the scaffolding shimmer appears, indicating the novel framings are unreadable rather than transfer-hard; (b) children brute-force by incrementing the bundle-count dial one at a time and refiring until the span fills, indicating the interaction permits counting-on instead of equal-groups reasoning (mitigation: drift cost per fire should make this strategy visibly expensive — if it doesn't, the stakes design is falsified); (c) success rates on the disguised framings match the ghost-plank framing exactly, suggesting the framings aren't actually novel; or (d) engagement telemetry shows abandonment spikes at the gondola span, indicating the context switch broke comprehension rather than tested transfer.
